title: Payment Orchestration Platform
strapline: A timeout is not a failed payment.
excerpt: Separating payment intent from provider attempts, so retries and late confirmations don't create a second charge.
question: What happens when the provider accepts a payment, but the response never arrives?
problem: A checkout request crosses a boundary the application cannot control. If a provider times out after accepting it, blindly retrying through another provider can turn a network problem into a duplicate charge.
approach: Give the payment intent one owner. Persist the merchant-scoped idempotency key and request fingerprint before starting a provider attempt. Treat an ambiguous response as awaiting confirmation, then use a verified webhook or reconciliation result to resolve it.

flow.name: Merchant API
flow.details: Authenticate merchant; validate amount and key.

flow.name: Payment domain
flow.details: Own intent, attempt history and legal transitions.

flow.name: Provider adapter
flow.details: Translate requests; classify definite vs ambiguous failures.

durableBoundary: PostgreSQL: payment intent + request fingerprint + attempt + outbox record. Unique merchant/key constraint. Never hold a database transaction open across a provider call.
asyncBoundary: Outbox relay → SQS → attempt worker. Verified webhooks enter an inbox; reconciliation resolves missing confirmations. Each consumer deduplicates independently.

decisions.title: Separate intent from attempts
decisions.choice: A merchant payment can have several traceable attempts, but an unresolved attempt prevents blind rerouting.
decisions.cost: Lower apparent availability during uncertainty; operational reconciliation is required.

decisions.title: Provider-specific idempotency
decisions.choice: Reuse a provider key for the same attempt, only where the provider guarantees that behaviour. Store the relationship locally.
decisions.cost: Providers have different key retention and retry contracts. An abstraction cannot erase those differences.

decisions.title: Start with a modular service
decisions.choice: Keep domain, adapter and webhook modules explicit inside one Spring Boot service before introducing more deployable services.
decisions.cost: Less independent scaling initially, but simpler transaction boundaries and incident investigation.

operations.title: Unknown outcomes
operations.body: Alert on age of awaiting-confirmation payments, not just HTTP error rates. Route unresolved items to a reconciliation queue with evidence.

operations.title: Safe recovery
operations.body: Bound retries for definitively retryable failures. Dead-letter exhaustion for review. Never replay a financial operation without checking its current state.

operations.title: Trust boundary
operations.body: Verify provider signatures and replay windows before inbox insertion. Redact tokens and sensitive payloads; retain correlation IDs and audit metadata.

demo.title: The response was lost. Now what?
demo.description: Submit a simulated CAD 75.00 payment, retry the request, then deliver its provider confirmation twice.
demo.limitation: Single payment, in-memory TypeScript model. The webhook is assumed verified. No provider calls, persistence, concurrency or signature verification.

outcome: The model keeps the provider attempt count at one when the request is retried, applies a confirmation once, and rejects reuse of an intent with a different amount. Those are tested local invariants, not a production reliability claim.
next: Implement PostgreSQL constraints and concurrency tests against a provider stub.
Test crash recovery around the outbox relay and webhook inbox.
Define retention, reconciliation SLAs and per-provider retry policies before a real integration.

title: Money Movement & Ledger
excerpt: Holds, settlement and reversals modelled as balanced journal entries, not destructive balance updates.
question: Can every balance change be explained, even after a reversal?
problem: A mutable balance says how much is there now, but not why. Holds, settlements and reversals become difficult to investigate when each operation overwrites the last result or publishes an event separately from its database commit.
approach: Represent each money movement as a balanced transaction in an append-only journal. Separate available funds from held funds. Settle from the hold, release an unused hold, and reverse a settlement with compensating entries rather than editing history.

flow.name: Command API
flow.details: Validate currency, amount, identity and command key.

flow.name: Ledger transaction
flow.details: Lock affected accounts in a stable order; enforce funds and balanced postings.

flow.name: Read models
flow.details: Expose available, held and settled views with a projection version.

durableBoundary: PostgreSQL: command receipt + journal transaction + postings + outbox record, committed together. One currency per transaction. Balance projections remain verifiable against the journal.
asyncBoundary: Outbox relay → event bus → reporting projections. Consumers track event IDs and account sequence numbers. An event stream is not a substitute for the accounting source of truth.

decisions.title: Integer minor units
decisions.choice: Use integer CAD cents in this model. A backend would use bounded integer or exact decimal storage with currency-specific precision.
decisions.cost: Multi-currency and FX require explicit rounding policies and balancing accounts. They are deliberately out of scope.

decisions.title: Serialize the conflicting writes
decisions.choice: Lock accounts in a consistent order within a short transaction and check available funds before posting.
decisions.cost: Hot accounts can bottleneck. Measure contention before introducing partitioning or more complex concurrency control.

decisions.title: Compensate, don't erase
decisions.choice: A reversal references the original settlement and posts the opposite entries.
decisions.cost: A longer journal, but the audit trail remains intelligible. Real reversals also need funds and policy checks.

operations.title: Accounting invariants
operations.body: Check that every transaction balances per currency and that stored balance projections agree with the journal. Investigate discrepancies rather than auto-correcting history.

operations.title: Delivery lag
operations.body: Monitor oldest unpublished outbox event and projection lag. Expose read freshness instead of presenting stale data as authoritative.

operations.title: Recovery boundaries
operations.body: Rebuild projections from the journal. Test backup restoration and replay on isolated data before allowing operator recovery actions.

demo.title: Follow the money, entry by entry.
demo.description: Start with a fictional CAD 1,000.00 balance. Hold CAD 250.00, settle or release it, and inspect a reversal.
demo.limitation: One account pair and one transfer in browser memory. Signed postings illustrate conservation; this is not a full chart of accounts, database transaction or deployable financial ledger.

outcome: The executable model derives balances from its journal. Each operation adds two offsetting entries, duplicate commands do not post again, and a reversal preserves the original settlement. Tests cover those properties and invalid transitions.
next: Implement durable command receipts and concurrent spend tests with PostgreSQL.
Add partial settlement, hold expiry and explicit reversal constraints.
Test outbox redelivery, projection rebuilding and single-currency accounting reconciliation.

title: Architecture Decision Hub
strapline: Keep the reasoning, not just the result.
excerpt: Versioned decisions with explicit ownership, review boundaries and a record of the trade-offs a team accepted.
question: Six months later, can the team still explain why a decision was made?
problem: Architecture decisions often disappear into chat threads. New engineers see the implementation without its constraints, accepted risks or the conditions that should trigger a revisit. A stale approval can also endorse a proposal that has changed since review.
approach: Keep a small decision record: context, alternatives, decision, consequences, owner and review trigger. Version it. Require review against the current revision, preserve superseded decisions, and link operational learnings back to the assumptions they challenge.

flow.name: RFC workspace
flow.details: Markdown proposal, alternatives, owner and affected systems.

flow.name: Decision workflow
flow.details: Validate identity, revision and allowed state transition.

flow.name: Decision history
flow.details: Accepted and superseded records remain addressable.

durableBoundary: PostgreSQL: versioned record + review evidence + risk links. Compare expected revision in the update predicate, then append audit history within the same transaction.
asyncBoundary: After commit, notifications and a search index can update independently. Search results point to the canonical record; a stale index never authorizes a workflow transition.

decisions.title: Short records over a document portal
decisions.choice: Use a consistent Markdown structure and links to existing diagrams and incidents.
decisions.cost: Less structured reporting, but a lower writing burden. An unused workflow creates no institutional memory.

decisions.title: Review the exact revision
decisions.choice: Reject stale updates and require a reviewer distinct from the owner for acceptance.
decisions.cost: Some updates need a second review. That friction is intentional at the acceptance boundary.

decisions.title: Human judgment remains authoritative
decisions.choice: Store evidence, risks and revisit triggers without calculating a synthetic architecture quality score.
decisions.cost: The tool cannot decide whether a trade-off is good. The team still needs a useful review habit.

operations.title: Ownership drift
operations.body: Surface accepted decisions without an active owner or with overdue review triggers. Escalate through the team's normal ownership process.

operations.title: Access and content
operations.body: Apply authorization at each API boundary. Render Markdown without raw HTML by default; do not put secrets or incident customer data into decision records.

operations.title: Workflow evidence
operations.body: Log who changed which revision and why. Preserve audit history on supersession and export records in a format the team can keep without this tool.

demo.title: A reviewer has an old version open.
demo.description: Submit a draft, attempt a stale approval, and then accept the current revision as the reviewer.
demo.limitation: A deterministic workflow model with simulated roles. No identity provider, persistence, collaborative editing or server-side authorization is implemented here.

outcome: The model rejects stale revisions, blocks owner self-approval and preserves an ordered history through acceptance and supersession. It demonstrates a workflow boundary, not a claim of organizational adoption.
next: Implement server-derived roles and atomic version checks in PostgreSQL.
Add Markdown rendering tests and access-control tests for linked records.
Pilot the record format with a small team before adding search or notification infrastructure.
